| Metabolomic analysis of Xanthine dehydrogenase mutants in Bacteria         |

# Introduction

Nitrogen is the most abundant gas accounting for 78% of the air and is essential for life. However, due to its triple bond, its use cannot be from the gaseous form for most organisms including plants. But bacteria developed an enzyme, nitrogenase that can convert N2 to ammonia which is assimilable for the plants. That is why, plants from the legumes family can form root nodule symbiosis, where nodules are specialised organs that contain N-fixing bacteria. _Medicago truncatula_ is a model plant from the Inverted Repeat-Lacking Clade (IRLC) that form indeterminate nodules. In this interaction, the plant secretes nodule-cysteine rich (NCR) peptides that helps terminally differentiate bacteria into bacteroids. (Udvardi & Poole, 2013). Bacteroids are the form which is highly effective in nitrogen fixation and only do endoreplication.

Purines are recognized as the universal and essential building blocks of DNA and RNA, structurally conserved from bacteria to humans. In addition to their importance in nucleic acid synthesis, purine catabolism is also essential, allowing organisms to excrete excessive nitrogen, under the form of species-specific metabolites. In bacteria, this catabolic pathway leads to the production of uric acid, an intermediate metabolite the bacteria can reinject in its metabolism to recycle nitrogen.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1: Assembly of xanthine dehydrogenase (Schumann et al., 2008)

Xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH) is a conserved enzyme that is part of the purine metabolism. Its role is to convert hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid (Zrenner et al., 2006). This enzyme can be converted to xanthine oxidase (XO) either in a reversible way by oxidation of the sulfhydryl residues or irreversibly by proteolysis. The latter form can produce more ROS compared to XDH as it uses O<sub>2</sub> as a substrate instead of NAD (Enroth et al., 2000). XDH has a (αβ)<sub>2</sub> heterotetrameric structure (Figure 1) (Schumann et al., 2008). There are three different subunits to make the enzyme functional. XDHA1 is bound to two non-identical \[2Fe2S\] clusters and FAD whereas XDHB1 is bound to the sulfurated form ofthe molybdenum cofactor (Moco).

There are two copies of the genes in the genome of _E. meliloti_. _xdhA2_ and _xdhB2_ are located within a single operon that also encodes the _bdhA_ gene, which is important in the Poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate (PHB) cycle (carbon and energy reserve). The second copy of these genes are also within a single operon, which encodes _xdhA1, xdhB1_ and _xdhC_. _xdhC_ is believed to encode a chaperone essential to form the functional enzyme. (Walsh, 2010) The enzyme can be composed of units from the same operon or from the two (ex. XDHA1/XDHB2). Neither cluster can form a functional, active XDH enzyme without the _xdhC_ gene.

XDH mutants were chosen after a pull-down experiment from the Reinhardt's lab, where they tried to see the interaction between protein isolated from either free-living bacteria or bacteroids and NCR peptides. Thus, they observed that XDH has high interaction with various NCRs and were curious for their implications in the symbiosis. In addition, it is known that uric acid and its derivatives can be used for storing and transporting nitrogen. (Zrenner et al., 2006). For example, in soybean with _Bradyrhizobium japonicum_, ureides are the major form to transport the fixed nitrogen from nodules to the rest of the plant. (Nguyen et al., 2023) In their study, Nguyen and al. also observed that when mutating the XDH of the plant the symbiosis was defective.

# Data processing

## Sample preparation

1 scoop of bacteria from glycerol stock (-70 °C) were added to a flask containing TY media with antibiotics (20 mL, 20 μL of streptomycin and 20 μL of kanamycin for the mutants, only streptomycin for the wild type). The bacteria were grown for 48 hours at 28°C and shaken at 180 min<sup>\-1</sup>. The optical densities (OD) of the cultures were measured, but as they were around 1 (meaning around the end of the exponential phase), they were first conserved in a pellet (not resuspended) in 7.5 mL of TY for 72 hours. Then, 500 μL of the liquid culture, where the pellet was still not dissolved, was added in TY (20 mL and the antibiotics). They were left 24 hours to grow in the same conditions mentioned before, and the OD were measured again.

The OD were the following:

| Name         | Replicate a | Replicate b | Replicate c | Replicate d |
| ------------ | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| WT           | 0.50        | 0.51        | 0.53        | 0.52        |
| _xdhA1_ (11) | 0.62        | 0.65        | 0.69        | 0.65        |
| _xdhB1_ (4)  | 0.96        | 0.99        | 0.98        | 0.98        |
| _xdhA2_ (8)  | 0.49        | 0.81        | 0.69        | 0.59        |

As the cultures of _xdhB1_ grew faster than the others, 1 mL of the cultures were added to TY media (20 mL and the antibiotics) and grew for 8 hours until the OD were the following:

| Name        | Replicate a | Replicate b | Replicate c | Replicate d |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| _xdhB1_ (4) | 0.66        | 0.71        | 0.75        | 0.59        |

When they had the expected OD, the liquid cultures were centrifuged for 10 minutes at 5000 rpm to form pellet. The TY medium was removed, and the pellet were washed three times with saline solution (NaCl 0.85% v/v). Finally, the pellets were flash freezed and conserved at -70 °C until further use.

## Metabolites extraction

To extract metabolites, 1mL of extraction solution (AC/H2O (80/20) + 0.1% FA was added to each sample to resuspend the pellet before vortexing. Once resuspended, samples were transferred to a new ED, with 3 beads inside.

The ED tubes were placed on the bead shaker, with a program altering break for 20 seconds (frequence = 29/s). They were finally centrifugated 5' at 16'000 RCF. Finally, 200 uL of each sample were collected and placed in a final vial. Quality control (QC) was also prepared by mixing 20uL of each sample, including the blank.

## Data acquisition

The samples, QC and the blank (18 total) were analyzed by a Liquid Chromatography coupled to a Mass-Spectrometer (LC-MS). The Liquid Chromatography was performed with Reversed phase C18 and Hydrophilic Interaction Liquid Chromatography (HILIC) columns.

## Data treatment

Raw data were imported and converted into a mzXML format using Proteowozard software. The files were then treated with MzMine and processed with the following workflow:

- Isolation of the significant MS peak from the background noise, selected from lower peaks on the LC plot (MS1 noise level=1.0E5, MS2 noise level=0).
- Reconstruction of individual chromatographic peaks based on their retention times using the ADAP Chromatogram Builder (MS1, polarity=+, minimum consecutive scan=8, m/z tolerance=0.0020 m/z, minimum intensity for consecutive scans=minimum absolute height=1.0E5).
- Chromatogram deconvolution by mathematically distinguishing two molecules that are eluting at the same time (minimum search range RT/Mobility = 0.050, Min ratio of peak top/edge=1.70, peak duration range=0-2min/mobility, minimum scans=5).
- Groupment of isotopes (m/z tolerance=0.0010m/z, retention time tolerance=0.02, maximum charge=2).
- Feature alignment to ensure a comparison between the samples (m/z tolerance = 0.0010, weight for m/z=20, retention time tolerance=0.10, weight for RT=20, mobility weight=1).
- Isotope filter to eliminate signals that do not exhibit a consistent or sufficient isotopic profile (minimum aligned samples, minimum signals in an isotope pattern, never remove rows with MS2, require MS2 scan)
- Normalization step to correct technical variations using total ion current (TIC)
- Gap filling to reanalyze raw data and ensure the accuracy of the measure (Intensity tolerance=30%, m/z tolerance=0.001, retention time tolerance=0.05, minimum scans=5).

# Results and discussion

_NB: due to a misannotation, the_ XDH _mutants appear under the name_ xth _in the graphs._

After the data treatment, 457 features were identified. They are clustered by Cytoscape in 1142 nodes and 1832 edges.

![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2: Cytoscape clustering

At a first glance, some clusters are only composed of _XDHB1's_ metabolites*,* but when looking at the structure very few of them had the gnps proposition. This already suggests that _XDHB1_ might be different from the others.

## PCA

PCA (Principal Component Analysis) is a powerful tool used to simplify large datasets. This tool is used to reduce complexity while maintaining essential information. PC1 and PC2, shown on the y and x axes, summarize the biggest patterns in our dataset. PC1 shows the largest source of variation, while PC2 shows the second largest source of variation.

According to PCA Figure 3, we can clearly see that the _XDHA1_ and _XDHA2_ mutants conserve more similar properties compared to the wild type. On the other hand, _XDHB1_ is positioned differently, which means that it preserves different properties compared with the others. In our case, we observe PC1 = 59.6% and PC2 = 11.8% of variance. The _XDHB1_ mutant cluster tightly on the far-right side of PC1 indicating a clearly distinct from WT, _XDHA1_, and _XDH_A2. WT and \_XDHA1_(orange) overlap considerably, while _XDHA2_ (cyan) overlaps partially with WT and _XDHA1_ on PC1 but has a much larger spread along PC2. According to this observation, the XDHB1 mutation produces the strongest global effect in the dataset.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3: PCA in HILIC

In the 3D PCA, the third principal component (PC3) is included, explaining an additional source of variation and making the observations clearer (Figure 4). Comparing the 3D PCA with the 2D PCA, overlap between _XDHA1_, _XDHA2_, and WT still occurs. _XDHB1_ still occupies an individual position, which further strengthens this observation.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 4: 3D PCA

## Volcano plot about families

A volcano plot is a special kind of scatterplot designed to easily and quickly identify statistically significant changes between two conditions. It is typically used to screen for genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics data to find genes, proteins, and metabolites whose expression or quantity varies between the two conditions being analyzed.

In our case, the volcano plot consists of a Y-axis, which represents the magnitude of change between the two conditions (Log2 of the difference between the two conditions), while the X-axis represents the -Log10 of the P-value and indicates the statistical significance. Consequently, the relevant data are located in the upper right and left quadrants and are those showing a large magnitude change and are statistically significant.

![](data:image/png;base64,)As shown in Figure 5, the data reveal that, compared to the WT, the _XDHA1_ mutant exhibits few differences in the fold change among the various metabolites. Among these, hypoxanthine stands out, as it is present in higher concentrations in the _XDHA1_ mutant. The absence of one of the two copies of xanthine dehydrogenase results in a reduced hypoxanthine metabolism and, consequently, higher concentrations of this compound.

Figure 5: Volcano plot WT vs XDHA1

Figure 6 is more interesting, as it shows that the _XDHA2_ mutant has significantly higher levels of many metabolites compared to the WT, including hypoxanthine. This marked difference between _XDHA1_ and _XDHA2_ likely indicates that these two copies of the same gene have probably different functions or varying levels of activity or expression.![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 6: Volcano plot WT vs XDHA2

![](data:image/png;base64,)Figure 7 shows a significant difference between WT and _XDHB1_; many metabolites are enriched in _XDHB1_, including hypoxanthine and other purines. This appears to indicate a slowed purine metabolism with possible repercussions on other metabolic pathways. The change here appears much more dramatic than in the other conditions analysed, with purine metabolism likely impaired to a greater extent compared to _XDHA1_ and _XDHA2_ mutants.

Figure 7: Volcano plot WT vs XDHB1

## Tree map

A tree map (Figure 8) represents the chemical composition of metabolites by grouping them into chemical classes and visualizing their relative abundances. Each rectangle represents a metabolite feature, where the rectangle's size reflects relative abundance, and the color indicates the group in which the metabolite is enriched. Dark blue rectangles represent metabolites enriched in WT, while light blue rectangles represent metabolites enriched in the _XDHB1_ mutant.

Based on the largest metabolite clusters and the strongest color shifts, glycerophospholipids and linear polyketides were selected for further analysis, as these groups appeared to contribute most strongly to the metabolic differences between WT and _XDHB1_.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 8: Treemap WT vs XDHB1

**Glycerophopholipids**

Within the glycerophospholipid group, the darkest rectangle, representing a metabolite enriched in WT, corresponded to feature 244 (m/z: 704.487, RT: 1.335). According to CANOPUS annotation, this metabolite belongs to the fatty acid biochemical pathway and is classified as a glycerophospholipid, more specifically an oxidized glycerophospholipid.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The brightest rectangle within this group, representing enrichment in the _XDHB1_ mutant, corresponded to feature 242 (m/z: 718.502, RT: 1.319). Similar to feature 244, this metabolite was classified within the fatty acid biochemical pathway and glycerophospholipid superclass; however, it was more specifically annotated as a glycerophosphocholine.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Glycerophospholipids are important components of the plasma membrane and play essential roles in multiple cellular functions. Glycerophospholipid remodeling and diversity contribute to lipid homeostasis regulation, maintenance of membrane fluidity, stress response mechanisms, signal transduction, and vesicle trafficking. An enrichment of oxidized glycerophospholipids in WT may indicate normal membrane integrity. In contrast, the enrichment of glycerophosphocholine-related metabolites in the _XDHB1_ mutant may suggest stress adaptation, compensatory membrane remodeling, and altered phospholipid turnover. Considering these results, the following hypothesis could be formulated: the _XDHB1_ mutation seems to affect membrane-related metabolic processes and could induce changes in lipid homeostasis.

**Linear polyketides**

Linear polyketides were another metabolite group showing strong distribution differences between WT and _XDHB1_.

The darkest rectangle, representing a metabolite enriched in WT, corresponded to feature 417 (m/z 787.515, RT 2.278). This metabolite was putatively annotated as Exophilin B2. CANOPUS classification assigned this compound to the polyketide biochemical pathway, with linear polyketides as the broad chemical superclass and open-chain polyketides as the main chemical class.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The brightest rectangle, representing enrichment in the _XDHB1_ mutant, corresponds to feature 10 (m/z: 728.572, RT: 0.468). Although no compound identity could be assigned to this feature, CANOPUS classified it within the alkaloid biochemical pathway, while the broader chemical classification placed it within linear polyketides and more specifically open-chain polyketides.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Due to the wide range of polyketides localization and functions, it might be challenging to formulate a specific hypothesis.

## Metabolites (boxplot)

### Purine metabolism

As the mutants target the purine metabolism, specific metabolites in this pathway were investigated.

Hypoxanthine, identified as feature 475 (m/z: 137.0458, RT: 3.01), is accumulated in the mutants compared to WT (Figure 9). As the mutants cannot convert it to xanthine, it was expected to be more present in the mutants.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 9: Box-plot of feature 475 (m/z: 137.0458, RT: 3.01), hypoxanthine

Then, when focusing on xanthine identified in feature 647 (m/z: 135.0302, RT: 4.16), we can see that it is accumulated in the mutant _XDHB1_ (Figure 11). Xanthine is not only produced by the XDH. There are two other pathways (Figure 10): from the conversion of xanthosine with Inosine-guanosinenucleosidase or from the conversion of guanine with Guanine deaminase. (Zrenner et al., 2006) .

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 10: Purine metabolism; synthesis pathways for xanthine

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 11: Box plot of feature 647 (m/z: 135.0302, RT: 4.16), xanthine

When looking for uric acid nothing was found. However, the feature 497 (m/z: 153.0407, RT: 2.8) corresponds to 8-hydroxyxanthine which is a tautomeric form of uric acid (enol form). On the Figure 12, it was present in the WT and the _XDHA_ mutants but not in the the _XDHB1_ mutant.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 12: Box plot of feature 497 (m/z: 153.0407, RT: 2.8), 8-hydroxyxanthine

The feature 543 (m/z: 186.039, RT: 3.04) is also interesting as it was identified to pterin (2-Amino-4-hydroxypteridine) which can chelate a molybdenum atom to form the Molybdenum Cofactor (MoCo). As explained in the introduction, MoCo is bound to the XDHB1 units. As seen on Figure 13, it is accumulated in WT and in the two XDHA mutants, but absent in XDHB1. As the XDHB1 is not functional, maybe the compound is downregulated, because it cannot be assembled into a holoprotein. However, it should be noted that the sirius confidence score is only 12%.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 13: feature 543 (m/z: 186.039, RT: 3.04), 2-amino-4-hydroxypteridine

After these results, the following hypothesis can be formulated: _XDHA_ mutants may still be partially functional and convert some hypoxanthine to xanthine. On the other hand, xdhB1 would be nonfunctional and to compensate for the lack of xanthine, other pathways can be upregulated. For instance, some guanine derivatives are present in higher amount in _XDHB1_ such as N7-(2-Hydroxyethyl)guanine identified in feature 509 (m/z: 196.0829, RT: 2.87) and 7-(2'-carboxyethyl)guanine identified in feature 409 (m/z: 206.0673, RT: 2.25). To further indicate the partial functioning of _XDHA1_ and _XDHA2_, it is worth noting that the tautomeric form of uric acid is present in higher concentrations in the _XDHA_ mutants and absent in _XDHB1_, and that the XDH is the only enzyme identified to convert xanthine to uric acid.

### Stress

As part of Théana's master's thesis, it was also interesting to study the impact of mutations on bacterial stress. In the MS results, some metabolites have been identified as stress specific compounds and 2 are presented here.

The feature 687 corresponds to the glycine betaine (m/z: 140.068 and RT: 4.241) and corresponds to the pathway of Amino acids and Peptides. The relative quantitative abundance across the different mutants is represented in the boxplot (Figure 14), in which only the _XDHB1_ mutant shows a significant decrease.

Glycine betaine is known for its osmoregulation action. Some previous studies showed its importance in the resistance against abiotic stress (Hussain Wani et al., 2013). A decreased of this compound in the metabolome of the mutant _XDHB1_ would indicate an alteration to stress response and the associated metabolism.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 14: Boxplot of feature 687 (m/z: 140.068 and RT: 4.241), glycine betaine

The other metabolite, feature 342 (m/z: 688.455 RT: 1.94), corresponds to an oxidized glycerophosphocholine (PC). In a similar pattern as feature 687 (see Figure), this metabolite seems to be less abundant in the mutant _XDHB1_, regarding the relative quantitative abundance of the different mutants (Figure 15).

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 15: Boxplot of feature 342 (m/z: 688.455 RT: 1.94), oxidized glycerophosphocholine

This type of fatty acid is involved in the membrane, and the oxidation state of the metabolite suggests a potential oxidative stress for the bacteria (Naguib et al., 2022). The low abundance of PC in _XDHB1_ mutant highlights a potential membrane redistribution to provide its survival.

Given these results, we might wonder if the bacteria, specifically the _XDHB1_ mutant, reallocates its metabolism, rather than just its purine metabolism, to optimize its growth.

# Conclusion

In this metabolomic experiment, we observed that the _XDHB1_ mutant seems to stand out and be more different than the WT and the _XDHA_ mutants. It was visible from the PCA, the clusters or more into details with the box plots. These results correspond to the screening made by Théana, in which phenotypically _XDHB1_ nodules were different from the WT and the _XDHA._

From the box plot, it seems that _XDHB1_ is non-functional, and XDHAs might be partially functional. That would explain why _XDHB1_ is more different. In addition, due to the presence of glycerophospholipides and compounds linked to stress, this suggests that a mutation in the purine metabolism also affects other metabolic aspects, indicating a large impact.

However, our results should be taken with a grain of salt, because _XDHB1_ mutants also have additional manipulation, increasing variability, as they grew faster than the rest of the mutants. Hence, this experiment should be redone, and it could also be interesting to add the _XDHB2_ and _XDHC_ mutants to compare the results. Another improvement could be the use of standards for xanthine and uric acid, to ensure that the features correspond.
